title: Text blocks as case labels

blocks.text: The page says a text block is an ordinary `String`: it is interned like any literal, and a text block constant can be a `case` label. It also says a literal and a text block with the same characters are even `==`, *because both are compile-time constants*. A string built while the program runs is not.
Write `Replies.reply(String message)`. The starter declares the known messages as text block constants. The answer is:

The message may come from anywhere: a literal, a `StringBuilder`, a `formatted()` call or `null`. It matches a known message when it has exactly the same characters, so neither `"Hello
World
"` nor `"hello
world"` is `HELLO`, and a `null` message is `"unknown"`.

cases.says: Each known message, written as a literal, gets its reply, and any other message gets "unknown".
A message built at run time, with the same characters as a known one, gets the same reply.
A message that differs only by a trailing newline is a different message.
A null message gets "unknown" instead of throwing.

concepts: A text block constant can be a case label in a switch on a String.
Text blocks are interned like literals: a text block and a literal with the same characters are ==, but a string built at run time is not.
